studies.title: The Moon And The Second Explanation
studies.meaning: Two events are joined by a single conjunction, the Hour approaching and the moon splitting, so the sign is presented as a piece of the end already arriving. Most classical commentators read the splitting as something that happened at Mecca and was seen; a minority read it as a description of the Hour itself. The response is then given as a habit rather than a decision. Whatever they see, they turn from it and call it magic that keeps on coming. The verdict is that what reached them was already sufficient.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the leadership had settled into open rejection. The classical sources report with unusual agreement that the moon was seen to split at Mecca and that the objection raised was enchantment of the eyes. The surah that follows is built for an audience that has already refused: it argues by example rather than by proof, running through five destroyed peoples at speed.

keyTerms.note: A verb of approach in a form that stresses the closing of distance. It puts the Hour in motion toward the listener rather than waiting at the end of time, which is why the ayah can pair it with something already seen.

The word can mean ongoing, and it can mean bitter, and commentators record both. Either way the objection concedes the event and reassigns it, which is what an explanation offered in place of a denial usually does.
From a root for driving something back with a shout. The news of earlier peoples is described not as information but as a thing that should have pushed the hearer away from where he was standing.

The adjective describes something that reaches its destination, as a traveller reaches a town. The phrase grades the message as complete at the point of delivery, so the ayah that follows can locate the failure at the other end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan calendar ran on the moon, and so did everything attached to it: the sacred months when fighting stopped, the fairs, the debts that fell due at a named new moon. Men watched for the crescent as a matter of business. A caravan leader could tell the night of the month by looking up. That habit of watching is what makes the sign in this ayah a public event rather than a private vision.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word of the second ayah and the last word of the third differ by one consonant. One means continuing without stopping; the other means settling into its final place. The surah sets the objectors' description of the sign beside God's description of every affair, and the two words rhyme because they are built on the same pattern.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is granted and it changes nothing, and the passage does not treat that as a puzzle. Evidence is presented as insufficient by itself, because the obstacle named is not a missing proof but a following of inclination. That has a consequence for anyone waiting to be convinced. It also sets the terms for the rest of the surah, which offers no further argument and instead asks six times whether anyone is willing to take the point.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle directly: a granted sign does not produce belief when the will is set against it.
Gives the reason signs were withheld from later peoples, which is the other half of what this passage assumes.
Opens another surah with the same verb of approach and the same turning away in the next clause.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you have said would settle a question for you: a result, a conversation, an answer. Then look back at something you already got and did not let change your mind. You do not need to conclude anything about it. Just notice how quickly the mind supplies a second explanation, because that reflex is what this passage is describing.

studies.title: Called Out Like Locusts
studies.meaning: The instruction to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is to withdraw, not to argue further, and the scene that follows is what withdrawal leaves. A caller summons, and the dead come out of their graves with their eyes lowered. The simile chosen is a locust swarm: not frightening, but countless, disordered and moving as individuals. They hurry toward the voice with their necks stretched forward. The passage gives them the last word, and what they say is an observation about the day rather than a plea.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just recorded that a sign was seen and explained away, and this is the turn: argument stops and description begins. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. Resurrection was the single teaching the Meccan leadership found hardest to take seriously, and much of the early revelation answers it not with reasoning but with scenes a listener has to stand inside.

keyTerms.note: An intensive plural applied to eyes rather than to people. The same root gives the word for stillness in prayer, so the vocabulary of reverence is used here for a posture nobody chose.

A rarer word for graves than the one the Quran normally uses. Classical lexicographers connect it with a hollow or a pit, so the image is of an opening in the ground rather than of a marked resting place.
The word carries both speed and a fixed forward stare. It describes a body pulled toward something it does not want, which is why the Quran uses it of people summoned rather than of people arriving.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Locust swarms were an Arabian fact, not an image. They arrived without warning, stripped a season's grazing in a morning, and then were gathered in sacks and eaten, since locusts were ordinary food. What a listener pictured was not menace but numbers without order: a ground covering of separate creatures, each moving on its own, none of them in formation, impossible to count and impossible to stop.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran stages this scene twice using the same rare word for graves. In surah 70 the dead come out at a run; here they come out like a locust swarm. Only three ayat in the Book use that word, and all three place it at the moment of emergence rather than at burial.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is presented here as a summons rather than as a natural process. Someone calls and the dead answer, which makes the event relational instead of mechanical. The detail that decides the passage is the direction of movement: they run toward the voice. Nobody is dragged at this stage. The humiliation is in the eyes, not in the legs, so what is described is a compliance that arrives too late to be worth anything.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same emergence with the same rare word for graves, replacing the swarm with a race toward a marker.
Has the trumpet blown and the dead sliding out of their graves toward their Lord, without the humiliation.
Uses the same word for hurrying with outstretched necks, and adds that their gaze does not return to them.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the next time you are called by name and you do not want to answer: a manager, a parent, a message you have been leaving unopened. Notice the two seconds between hearing it and moving. The passage is built on exactly that gap, and it is the only part of the scene you can still do anything about.

studies.title: A Prayer Of Three Words
studies.meaning: Noah's people are given one line of speech and one word of verdict: they called him mad, and he was driven off. His answer is not an argument but an appeal, and in Arabic it runs to three words. What follows is symmetrical. The sky is opened and the earth is split, and the two waters meet. The last clause insists the meeting was on a matter already measured out, so the flood is presented as an appointment kept rather than as an outburst.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the first of five compressed accounts of destroyed peoples that give the surah its shape, and Noah's is the longest of them. No specific occasion is reported. The surah belongs to the years when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was being called mad in Mecca by men who had known him since childhood, which is the word this passage puts in the mouths of Noah's people.

keyTerms.note: The verb shares its root with the word for a deterrent four ayat earlier. The same force that should have pushed the audience back from their position was instead used to push the messenger away.
A passive participle from the verb to overpower. Noah does not describe his people or their crime. He states his own position in one word, and the word he chooses concedes that he has lost.
Used of water that comes continuously and without gaps, the way tears are described. Placed after the opening of gates, it turns the sky from a barrier into a channel.
From the root for measuring and apportioning. The flood is not called large; it is called exact, and the same root returns near the end of the surah to describe everything that was created.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water in Arabia arrived from two directions and both were watched. Rain came rarely and hard, and a wadi could run within minutes of a storm on high ground miles away. Springs and wells were the other source, dug and owned and fought over. A man who heard of the sky opening and the ground bursting at once was hearing his two supplies, the scarce ones he prayed for, arriving together and not stopping.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran never tells the flood the same way twice. Here the sky's gates open and the ground breaks into springs; in surah 11 the signal is an oven welling up with water; in surah 23 the instruction is to load the ark when that happens. Each account supplies a detail the others leave out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a three word prayer beside a global event and treats them as one sequence. Nothing is said about whether the appeal was deserved or how it was weighed. The answer simply follows. Then the final clause withdraws the impression that the prayer caused the flood, since the waters met on a matter already decided. Both things are left standing: the appeal was real, and the timing was not improvised.

crossReferences.why: Records the same appeal from the other side, saying he called and was answered and rescued from the great distress.
Gives the flood's signal and the loading of the ark, the detail this account leaves out.
Preserves the longer form of Noah's prayer in the surah named after him.

studies.applyIt: Say something short the next time you are out of your depth. Not a composed prayer, not a list. Name the situation in one clause and ask for help in the next, the way this passage does. Then stop. Most people find the brevity harder than the asking, which is itself worth noticing about how you usually pray.

studies.title: Planks, Nails And A Refrain
studies.meaning: The ark is described by its materials, planks and nails, which keeps the miracle attached to an ordinary object. It sails under God's eyes. The reason given is repayment for a man who was rejected. Then two refrains begin that will run through the rest of the surah. One is a question about the punishment. The other is the statement that the Quran has been made easy for remembering. Scholars read that ease as ease of memorising and of understanding together.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that moves at speed through five destroyed peoples, giving each a few lines. No particular occasion is reported for these ayat. The surah belongs to the years when the Meccan leadership had rejected the message outright. Its shape is built to be spoken aloud: short lines, a hard rhyme, and two sentences that come back unchanged after each story.

keyTerms.note: A plural for the pegs or nails that hold planks together. Naming the fixings rather than the vessel is deliberate: the ark is described as a carpentry job, and the saving is attributed elsewhere.
A phrase of watching and of care together, used elsewhere of Moses as an infant and of the Prophet's endurance. It carries protection rather than surveillance, which the classical readers note.
An assimilated form of a word meaning one who remembers. It appears in this surah alone six times, always in the same question, and its sound is deliberately easy to say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had no shipwrights inland, but the Red Sea ports were full of them, and Meccan traders shipped goods from the coast. Everyone knew a hull was planks lashed and pegged, caulked against water that would find any gap. A boat was a thing you distrusted on principle. Describing the ark by its nails put Noah's rescue on a vessel the audience would have hesitated to board.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about the Quran being made easy for remembrance appears four times in this surah, once after each destroyed people. It appears nowhere else in the Book. The surah is built on repetition, which is itself a proof of the claim. The lines a listener has already heard three times are the ones that stay.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes the openness of revelation an act of God, not a property of the text or a talent in the reader. Ease is something done to the Book. That has a consequence the surah presses with its repeated question. If the difficulty has been removed, what is left in the way is willingness. The ark's description works the same way. Rescue arrives inside an ordinary wooden object, and the saving is credited to the eyes watching it.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same vessel being built, watched in the same phrase, while the people passing by laugh at it.
Repeats the claim of ease with a different image, revelation made light on the tongue that carries it.
Gives the length of the calling that preceded this rescue and names the ark as a sign for all peoples.

studies.applyIt: Memorise one short ayah this week, out loud, in the car or while washing up. Not a page. One ayah, until you can say it without checking. The surah's claim is that the Book has been made easy, and the only way to test a claim like that is on yourself, at the smallest possible scale.
studies.explainEasier: God carried Noah on a boat made of planks and nails. It sailed while God watched, as a reward for a man people had turned away. God left the story as a sign. He says he has made the Quran easy to remember.

studies.title: The Wind And The Question
studies.meaning: Aad get four ayat, the shortest of the five accounts. The punishment is named before it is described: a wind, and then a word for it that means howling and bitterly cold at once, on a day of unbroken misfortune. The simile is exact rather than grand. People are plucked up and left lying like the hollow stumps of uprooted palms. Then the refrain returns, and its question is not whether anyone heard but whether anyone is willing to remember.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The account of Aad follows Noah's and is deliberately shorter, since the surah is moving fast and expects its audience to know these peoples already. Aad were remembered in Arabian lore as a vanished southern nation of great stature and great building. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The refrain that closes them has already appeared once and will appear twice more.

keyTerms.note: A verb that means calling someone a liar rather than simply failing to believe. Four of the five accounts in this surah open with it, and each time the verb comes before the name of the people.
A doubled form built on a root for sound. Commentators divide over whether it names the noise of the wind or its extreme cold, and the records keep both readings in place rather than choosing.
A word from the vocabulary of luck, which pre-Islamic Arabs read in days and in the flight of birds. The Quran uses it here of a day whose character was fixed by what happened on it.
The first word names the lower part of the trunk, the heaviest section, and the adjective means torn out at the root. The comparison is to weight that was lifted anyway.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date palms were the capital of an oasis. A tree took years to bear and outlived the man who planted it, and its trunk was as fixed a point in a garden as a wall. Storms in the sand country could strip a settlement, and everyone had seen palms down after a bad night. What they had not seen was the root end lifted clear, which is the detail the ayah adds.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the wind here is used of only one people in the Quran, and it returns for them in two other surahs. Aad are the only nation in the Book destroyed by wind, and each account adds a measure: seven nights and eight days in one place, a wind that leaves nothing behind in another.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah does not argue that these events happened. It assumes them and asks a different question, which is whether knowing them changes anything. That shifts the burden from evidence to attention. Placing the refrain about the Quran's ease immediately after a destruction also makes a claim about how the Book works: the stories are not history to be learned but material made light enough to carry, so that only willingness stands between hearing and heeding.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same wind a duration, seven nights and eight days, and the same image of fallen palm trunks.
Supplies what this account omits, the boast of Aad that nobody was stronger than they were.
Tells the account at length, with the prophet sent to them and the exchange that preceded the wind.

studies.applyIt: Pick one story you have known since childhood, from the Quran or from your family, and ask what it would change if you took it as information about now. Say the answer out loud in one sentence. The refrain in this surah is not asking whether you have heard the account. It is asking whether hearing it has cost you anything.

studies.title: One Of Us, A Human Being
studies.meaning: Thamud's objection is quoted in full, and it is an argument about status rather than about truth. A single man, one of us, and we are to follow him. They conclude that doing so would put them in error and in madness, then ask why the reminder landed on him out of everyone. Their verdict is a lying braggart. The reply takes one ayah and does not engage the argument at all. It says they will find out tomorrow which side the word belongs to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud were the nearest of the destroyed peoples to Mecca, their rock-cut dwellings standing in the north of Arabia on the Syrian trade road and known by sight to caravan men. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The objection they raise, that a messenger should not be an ordinary man from among them, is the one the Meccan leadership raised in almost the same words.

keyTerms.note: The word names the human being as flesh and skin rather than as soul or mind. Putting it first in the sentence makes the objection turn on the body of the messenger, not on anything he said.
The word carries both a burning and a derangement, and the commentators record the two together. Thamud use it as an insult here, and the surah later returns the whole phrase to the guilty unchanged.

An adjective for someone swollen with his own importance. It is the second half of their charge, and the next ayah repeats both halves with the definite article, turning an insult into a description of someone specific.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leadership in Arabia was a matter of lineage and of what a clan could put in the field. A man's word carried the weight his family carried. To be asked to follow someone from your own group who held no seniority was to be asked to invert the order everything else depended on, including who spoke first at a council and who paid what in a blood settlement. The objection was social before it was theological.
studies.didYouKnow: Thamud describe their own imagined fate in two words, error and madness, if they were to follow a man like themselves. Twenty-three ayat later the surah uses the identical pair to say where the guilty actually are. That phrase occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and both of its occurrences sit inside this one chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records the standing objection to prophecy: that a messenger who eats and walks and belongs to a known family cannot be carrying anything from beyond. The Quran never answers it by making the prophet more than human. It answers by reframing the question as one about timing, saying only that tomorrow will show who was lying. Truth is left to be settled by outcome rather than by rank, which is itself a claim about how revelation is to be tested.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same objection and the messengers' reply that they are only human beings like the people they were sent to.
Puts the identical complaint in another nation's mouth, a man like yourselves who eats what you eat.
Explains why a human messenger is sent to human beings, and what would have been sent to angels instead.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you weigh advice by who gave it before you weigh what it said. A younger colleague, a sibling, someone whose life looks less sorted than yours. Take one thing you dismissed that way this month and look at the content alone, on paper, with the name removed. Then decide again.

studies.title: A Camel And A Timetable
studies.meaning: The she-camel is announced as a test, and the instruction to the prophet sent to Thamud is to watch and to hold out. What follows is administrative: the water is divided, each drinking turn attended in its own place. The whole trial is a rota. Then the collapse takes four words. They called their man, he took the thing in hand, and he hamstrung her. No motive is named and the act is given no build-up, which leaves the shortness of the interval doing the work.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Thamud's she-camel was among the best known signs in Arabian memory, and the surah assumes its audience knows the story and needs only its hinge. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The chapter gives the sign, the arrangement and the killing in four lines, where other surahs spend a dozen on the same events and include the warning that was ignored.

keyTerms.note: The root describes putting metal in fire to separate it from what is mixed in. A sign is called a trial here, which makes the miracle itself the difficulty rather than the relief.
An intensified form of the verb for patience, carrying effort rather than endurance alone. It is paired with a verb of watching, so the patience asked for is active attention over a set period.
A noun of apportioning used elsewhere for dividing up an inheritance. It places the shared spring in the vocabulary of shares and entitlements, which is the register the dispute actually belonged to.
The verb means cutting the leg tendons, the standard way of bringing a camel down before slaughter. It is the technical word, and using it keeps the act ordinary, which is part of the horror.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A well in a dry country ran on turns. Clans held named days at a spring, and the order was remembered, argued over and occasionally fought for. A beast that drank a whole day's water was not a curiosity but a competitor, and the arrangement here, one day for her and one for them, is exactly how a disputed source was managed. Hamstringing was how you ended a camel, done in the open with a blade.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran assigns the killing here to one man whom the others called forward, and elsewhere says the people as a whole hamstrung her. Commentators reconcile the two by noting that the group summoned him and consented, so the deed is recorded under both descriptions. Surah 91 compresses it furthest, into a single line about their most wretched being sent out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A sign is described as a trial rather than as a proof, which changes what a miracle is for. It does not settle the question; it raises the cost of the answer. The passage also shows a community deciding by delegation, calling one man forward so that the deed belongs to everyone and to nobody. That is why the punishment in the next ayah falls on all of them, and why both the singular and the plural accounts are preserved.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same episode at length, with the warning about touching her and the people acting as a single body.
Compresses it further still, naming the most wretched of them as the one who was sent forward.
Gives the drinking arrangement in the same terms, a day for her and a named day for you.

studies.applyIt: Think about a decision your group made that nobody in it would have made alone: a message sent, a person excluded, a corner cut. Work out who actually moved and who nodded. This passage is precise about that division and holds both sides of it. You do not need to reopen anything. Just be able to say, accurately, which part was yours.

studies.title: One Scream, Then Dawn
studies.meaning: Thamud end in a single sound. The word used is an ordinary cry, and what it leaves behind is compared to the dry broken fencing a pen-builder gathers and treads flat. The refrain follows, and then the fourth people arrive with the briefest introduction yet. Lot's people get one ayah of denial and one of consequence: stones sent down on them, with an exception cut into the middle of the same sentence for one household, brought out at the last hour before daylight.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The pace has been shifting throughout: Noah takes seven ayat, Aad four, Thamud nine, and Lot's people seven that begin here. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The cities associated with Lot lay on the caravan route north toward Syria, and the Quran elsewhere tells Meccan traders that they pass those ruins by morning and by night on their own journeys.

keyTerms.note: An ordinary word for a shout, used in the Quran for the sound that ends a people. Keeping it ordinary matters: what destroys Thamud is described with a word a shepherd would use of himself.
The image is the broken thorn fencing an owner piles round a fold, already dead and trodden down. Commentators differ over whether the second word names the man who builds it or the enclosure itself.

keyTerms.gloss: at the last of the night
keyTerms.note: The word names the hour just before dawn, the coldest and quietest stretch. It is the same hour the Quran elsewhere gives to those who ask forgiveness while it is still dark.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A sheep pen in Arabia was made of cut thorn, dragged in and stacked into a circle against predators. Within a season it dried, splintered and collapsed into a mat of grey fragments that got trodden into the ground. Every listener had walked over one. To be told a whole nation ended up looking like the rubbish round an old fold was to be given ruin with no grandeur left in it.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah fixes the rescue at the end of the night, and the same word appears in the Quran for those who seek forgiveness in the last dark. It is also the root behind the name of the meal taken before dawn in Ramadan. The account in surah 11 confirms the timing from the other direction, saying their appointed time was the morning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things happen inside one ayah and the order matters. The punishment is stated first and the exception second, cut into the sentence rather than added after it. That is how the Quran usually reports these events, and it makes the rescue part of the same act rather than a separate mercy arranged later. The passage also declines to describe the crime at this point, so the reader is given the shape of the outcome before any of the reasons.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same night and the same stones, with the appointed time named plainly as the morning.
States the exception in its barest form, saying only one house of those who submitted was found there.
Shows the visitors instructing Lot to travel in a portion of the night and not to look back.

studies.applyIt: Set one thing for the last hour before dawn this week, once. Not a whole night. Wake, drink water, say something short, go back to sleep. The Quran keeps returning to that hour for rescue and for asking, and it is the one part of the day you cannot get at by reading about it.

studies.title: Thus We Reward The Thankful
studies.meaning: The rescue is named a favour from Us and then generalised in a few words: this is how We repay whoever gives thanks. Gratitude is made the operative quality, not innocence and not belief in the abstract. The rest of the passage goes back to fill in what preceded the morning. He had warned them of a seizure and they argued over the warnings. They pressed him for his guests, and their sight was taken. The punishment that arrived at daybreak is called settled, a thing that stayed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These ayat close the account of Lot's people, and they are placed after the rescue rather than before it, so a listener learns the reason for the deliverance before learning what the city had done. No specific occasion is reported. Hospitality to a guest was the strongest obligation in Arabian custom, which is why the crime named here is framed as a demand made upon a host.

keyTerms.note: The word covers any good thing given without being owed. Applying it to a night escape rather than to wealth or rain widens it to include what did not happen to you, which is the harder half to notice.

The verb is left without an object, so the sentence names a quality rather than a particular act of thanks. Classical lexicons connect the root to an animal that yields much milk on very little fodder.
A noun for taking hold violently with the hand. It belongs to the vocabulary of a wrestler or an arresting officer rather than of a natural disaster, and it keeps the event personal.
The same word the surah used in its third ayah for every affair reaching its place. Here it describes a punishment that arrives and stays, so the two uses quietly frame the chapter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guest in Arabia was protected by the host's own standing. A man who could not keep his visitors safe was finished socially, and poems were made about households that fed strangers for three days without asking their names. Travellers moved between towns relying on nothing else. The demand described here is a demand against that whole system, which is why the account treats it as the point where a city stops being a city.
studies.didYouKnow: Every ayah in this surah ends on the same consonant, all fifty-five of them, closing on the letter that ends the word for moon in the opening line. Chapters of that length usually shift their rhyme at least once. The effect is that the refrains do not stand out as interruptions; to the ear they sound like the rest of the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is attached to a disposition rather than to a verdict. The passage does not say the household was innocent; it says they were thankful, and makes that the ground of the rule. Gratitude is therefore presented as the recognisable form of belief, the part that shows from outside. The account then supplies the contrast: a people who were warned, who disputed the warning, and whose final act was against a guest they should have been sheltering.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle as a promise, that thankfulness is met with increase while ingratitude carries its own consequence.
Gives the scene at the door which this passage refers to in a single clause.
Reports the city's answer to Lot and the rescue of his household, with the same exception attached.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing tonight that did not happen to you this year. Not a blessing you received; something you were spared and have mostly forgotten. Say it out loud once. This passage attaches rescue to gratitude, and the hardest gratitude to feel is for the thing that never arrived, because there is nothing in the house to point at.

studies.title: No Written Immunity
studies.meaning: Pharaoh's people take two ayat, the shortest of the five accounts in a chapter that has already spent nine on Thamud. They are given no speech and no scene. The warnings came, they denied every sign, and they were seized with the grip of one who is mighty and able. Then the surah turns from history to the room it is being recited in. Are your disbelievers better than those, or do you hold an acquittal written in the scriptures. Both questions expect no, and neither is answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah ends its sequence of destroyed peoples with the one its audience knew best from the trade routes and from the older scriptures, and gives it the least space. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. The direct address that follows is aimed at the Meccan leadership, who were claiming no written exemption; the question puts a claim in their mouths to show that nothing short of one could justify their confidence.

keyTerms.gloss: seizure by one mighty and able
keyTerms.note: The construction repeats the verb as a noun before naming the one who acts, a form Arabic uses for emphasis. The two names that follow pair unchallengeable standing with the actual power to use it.

A noun for being cleared of a claim, used of discharge from a debt or from liability for an injury. The question asks whether anyone holds a signed release, which is the only thing that would make their position reasonable.

A plural for books, from a root about writing something down firmly. The same word returns nine ayat later for the register in which every deed is kept, so the chapter asks about one record and answers with another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing existed in Arabia and mattered exactly where it was rare. Treaties were written and hung up, debts were recorded, and a document produced at the right moment settled what argument could not. Meccans knew that scriptures existed among the communities they traded with and that those communities set great store by what was written. A question about holding a written release lands hardest in a society where a written thing is unusual and decisive.
studies.didYouKnow: Pharaoh and Moses make up the most frequently retold narrative in the Quran, and here it is given two ayat with no dialogue at all. The surah reverses the usual proportions deliberately: the peoples an Arabian audience knew from their own landscape and their own roads receive the space, and the one they knew mainly from books gets a summary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns a series of historical reports into a general principle, and it does so by argument rather than by assertion. If earlier peoples were not spared, exemption would require either superiority or a document, and neither is available. What is denied is the sense of being a special case, which is a habit of mind rather than a doctrine. The surah treats that habit as the real obstacle, more durable than any objection said out loud.

crossReferences.why: Runs a similar list of destroyed peoples and closes by saying every one of them denied, so the threat was carried out.
Makes the same comparison, that God destroyed people mightier in force than the ones being addressed.
Records the same reliance on a supposed exemption, a punishment limited in advance to a few numbered days.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where you assume the ordinary rule does not apply to you. The deadline, the diet, the slow drift in a friendship that would worry you in someone else's life. Write the exemption out as a full sentence beginning with the words I am different because. Read it once. Most of them do not survive being written down.

studies.title: We Are A Winning Multitude
studies.meaning: A boast is quoted and answered in the next breath. They say we are a body that will not be beaten, and the reply puts the defeat in the future tense and adds the detail of backs turned. Commentators connect this to the rout at Badr, which came years after the words were first recited. Then the horizon changes. The real appointment is the Hour, given two comparatives: more calamitous, and more bitter. What follows is not a battle but the guilty in confusion, dragged on their faces.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, though these ayat are read alongside an event that had not yet happened. Classical sources report that the promise of a defeated multitude was recited in Mecca before the emigration and was understood only later, when the Meccan force was broken at Badr. The surah is otherwise addressed to a community under pressure and without power, which is the setting that makes a prediction of this kind worth making at all.

keyTerms.note: The first word is a mass gathered into one body, the second is someone who takes victory for himself. The boast is that number produces outcome, which is the assumption the following ayah removes.
A singular noun standing for a whole army's backs, which is how Arabic reports a rout. The same root gives the verb for considering a matter through to its end, following it to the back.
Two comparatives with nothing stated for comparison. The first names a disaster that outwits you, the second is a taste, so the pair joins the scale of the event to the way it is experienced.
One of several proper names the Quran gives the Fire, from a root about scorching and shrivelling skin. It occurs four times in the Book, and only two chapters use it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian warfare was decided by nerve rather than by tactics. Lines were loose, champions fought out in front, and a battle ended when one side broke and ran, which could happen within minutes and often to the larger force. Everyone had heard of a rout. Turning your back was the specific disgrace the poets named, worse than losing men, and a clan could carry the memory of one afternoon for generations.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given to the Fire at the end of this passage is left unexplained here. It appears in only one other surah, where the text stops to ask what it is before answering, a device the Quran reserves for a handful of terms whose weight it wants a listener to feel rather than simply learn.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses the scale the boast was made on. A defeat is promised, and then the promise is immediately relativised by something the speakers were not thinking about at all. That does two things at once: it says the near future will not go the way confidence suggests, and it says the near future is not the point in any case. Numbers are treated as the least reliable thing to lean on, because they are the easiest to count and the easiest to misread.

crossReferences.why: Shows the same confidence in numbers collapsing on the day itself, when the one who promised it withdraws.
Records a day when a large force was pleased by its own numbers and the numbers availed them nothing.
Names the same fire and pauses to explain it, which this passage deliberately does not.

studies.applyIt: Think of a plan you are confident about mainly because many people are behind it. A group opinion, a market, a family consensus. Write down the single strongest reason it could still be wrong, and keep it somewhere you will see it in a month. The passage does not say the crowd is always mistaken. It says the crowd is not the evidence.

studies.title: Measured, Instant, Written Down
studies.meaning: Three statements arrive in five ayat and each closes a different question. Everything created was made by a measure, which puts precision before power. The command is a single word and takes no longer than the flick of an eye, which removes any sense of process. And everything done is in the records, small and large alike. Between the second and third the surah asks for the last time whether anyone will take the point. The commentators hold the first to its plain sense: nothing created falls outside a measure.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has finished with its five peoples and turns to general statements, which is how many Meccan chapters close. No specific occasion is reported for most of these ayat, though classical sources preserve a well-known report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) came out to a group who were arguing about destiny and recited the first of them. The chapter's final refrain falls here, the sixth and last time the question is put.

keyTerms.note: The root covers measuring, apportioning and enabling. The preposition makes the measure the means of creation rather than a limit imposed on it afterwards, which is how the classical commentators read the phrase.

keyTerms.gloss: like a flick of the eye
keyTerms.note: The noun names the fastest movement an Arab could point at, the eye's glance. The comparison is not to speed of travel but to the smallest interval a person can actually measure by himself.
A passive participle from a root for ruled lines and rows, the same root behind the word for a line of writing. What is claimed is not memory but a record with an order to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Record keeping in Mecca was thin and mattered enormously. A merchant's ledger, a witnessed debt, the memorised genealogy of a clan: these were the only defences against a dispute years later, and men made their living by being reliable about them. Poetry did the rest of the remembering. To be told that every act, down to the smallest, sat in ruled lines somewhere was to be given the one filing system nobody could lose or bribe.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this passage uses for the records is the same one the surah used nine ayat earlier when it asked whether the Meccans held an exemption written in the scriptures. The chapter raises a question about one kind of written document and answers it by producing another, in which the reader appears rather than the ruling.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three attributes are set side by side and each qualifies the others. Measure without speed would suggest labour; speed without measure would suggest carelessness; both without a record would leave human action outside the account altogether. Together they describe a God for whom nothing is difficult and nothing is incidental. The passage also puts the human deed in the same frame as the created thing, so acting and being made are registered on the same terms.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing in other words, that He created everything and determined it with exact determination.
Gives the matter of the Hour as no more than the blink of an eye, or nearer than that.
Shows the record produced and opened, with the complaint that nothing small or large has been left out.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you treat as too small to count: a tone of voice at breakfast, a message you did not send, thirty seconds of attention given to someone. Choose one of them today and do it deliberately. The passage puts small and large into the same record, and the small is the only half you can change without planning anything.

studies.title: A Seat Of Truth
studies.meaning: The surah ends in two short ayat and the change of register is abrupt. After fifty-three lines of warning, the God-conscious are placed among gardens and a river, and then located more exactly: in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign who is able. That final phrase is what separates this from other descriptions of the garden. Nothing is said about food, shade or company. The reward described is a position, and the position is defined by who is near it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These are the closing ayat of a chapter that has spent its length on destroyed peoples and on the Hour, and they occupy a very small fraction of it. No specific occasion is reported. Brevity of this kind at the end of a warning surah is a common pattern in the Meccan revelations, where the last lines often turn without transition from the fire to the garden.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to shield or guard oneself. The word describes someone keeping a barrier between himself and harm, so it names a habit of care rather than a rank already achieved.

A place of sitting joined to the word for truthfulness, which in Arabic can describe a thing as genuine rather than counterfeit. The phrase occurs only here, and commentators read it as a station that will not turn out to be false.
An intensified form of the word for king, and the only place in the Quran it appears. Its indefinite ending functions as magnification in Arabic, so the effect is of a king beyond describing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Proximity was rank in Arabia. At a council or a feast, where you sat in relation to the chief was the public statement of your standing, and being moved up or down the circle was how honour was granted and withdrawn. Men remembered their place at a gathering for years afterwards. To describe the reward as a seat, and to fix it by whose presence it is in, was to use the one measure of status everyone there had felt.
studies.didYouKnow: The last word of the surah and the last word of the ayah about Pharaoh's people being seized are the same, a name describing the power to carry out what is intended. The chapter applies it once to a punishment and once to the company the righteous keep, so the closing note is not a different God from the one in the warnings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah has established God's power through five destructions and one seizure. These two ayat let that same power stand as the setting for the reward, which is a deliberate refusal to split the picture into a stern God and a kind one. The garden is described as nearness rather than as pleasure, and the word chosen for its truth suggests the difference from this world is not intensity but reliability: a place that does not turn out to be something else.

crossReferences.why: Describes the reward as something more than the reckoning, an addition the commentators read as the sight of God.
Gives the same closing move at much greater length, gardens and springs for those who fear their Lord.
Ends with the identical divine name, applied there to the seizure of Pharaoh's people rather than to the garden.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you sit this week. At a table, in a meeting, in a car. Notice who you choose to be near, and what that choice is doing for you. This ayah defines the final reward by proximity rather than by contents, and the habit it describes is one you already practise several times a day without calling it anything.
